title: Your account and the window
promiseText: Know what plan you're on and why, what the parts of the screen are, and where a conversation goes when you close it. Twenty minutes, once.
promiseHtml: Know what plan you're on and why, what the parts of the screen are, and where a conversation goes when you close it. Twenty minutes, once.
whyHtml:
The book said the setup lives here, so here it is. I kept it out of the chapters because this page goes stale faster than any other page in either book: plans change, buttons move, names change. Everything below is dated, and if the date is more than six months old, assume something has moved and look.

The reason to spend twenty minutes on this before Part A is simple. Every habit in the book assumes you know three things: which version of the tool you're paying for and what that buys you, where your conversations live, and what the panels on the screen are for. People who skip this spend their first month confused about why something they did yesterday isn't there today, and they blame themselves. Usually it's a setting.

Nothing here is a recommendation to pay. The free plan runs everything in Part A and most of Part B. Pay when you've hit a limit twice in a week and it cost you something; before that, the habits matter more than the tier.
exampleHtml:
I'm on a paid plan, because I use the tool for hours a day and I run the strongest model for most of it. [MARK: which plan, and the one reason you'd give a beginner for why.] I started on the free plan for the first few months, and that was the right call. The thing that pushed me up wasn't a feature. It was hitting the usage limit in the middle of a deck at 11 in the morning, twice in one week. I upgraded that afternoon.

My conversations live in two kinds of places. Most of them are inside projects (the book has one, the company has one), so they start already knowing what the work is. The rest are one-off rooms in the main list, and I treat those as disposable: if something in one turns out to matter, I move it into a project or write it into a file the same day. A conversation I can't find in a week is a conversation I should have filed.

yourTurn.question: Which plan are you on?
yourTurn.html: Which plan are you on? Write it down, and write the one limit you've hit so far, if any. (Two lines.)

yourTurn.question: What does your plan give you?
yourTurn.html: What does your plan give you? From the table in the sidebar below, copy the three things that matter for how you'll use the tool this month. (Three lines.)

yourTurn.question: Find the four parts of the window
yourTurn.html: Find the four parts of the window and write one phrase for what each is for, in your words:

fields.label: The panel that opens beside the chat when it makes something

yourTurn.question: Start a conversation and close it
yourTurn.html: Start a conversation and close it. Then find it again in the list. Write where it went. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Decide your rule
yourTurn.html: Decide your rule for one-off conversations: when something in one matters, where will you put it? (One sentence. Mine is above.)

howToHtml: How to: plans and the window, as of October 20, 2026, from claude.com/pricing and the Claude help center. Free: $0, Sonnet and Haiku models, web search, memory, connectors, file creation, up to five projects. Pro: $20 a month, or $17 on an annual plan; adds unlimited projects, the Opus model, the Fable model through usage credits, and the longer-running tools. Max: from $100 a month, five to twenty times Pro's usage. Team and Enterprise are priced per seat and add sharing and admin controls. Every plan has usage limits that reset on a rolling five-hour window; paid plans add weekly limits; there is no fixed message count, and Anthropic says plans and prices can change at its discretion. The window: your conversations and projects are in a sidebar on the left; the chat is in the middle; anything the tool builds (a document, a page, a deck) opens in a panel beside the chat and is also saved to an Artifacts tab in the sidebar; Settings is under your account name. Check the pricing page before relying on any number here.
compoundsHtml: You'll never think about the plan or the window again, which is the point. The twenty minutes here is spent once, and every page after it assumes you know where you are. The rule you wrote in question 5 is the first of the habits that keep your work from evaporating, and Worksheet 0.4 builds on it.

title: Files in, files out
promiseText: Attach a document, paste a passage, and download a result, so you know what the tool can read and what it can hand back. Fifteen minutes.
promiseHtml: Attach a document, paste a passage, and download a result, so you know what the tool can read and what it can hand back. Fifteen minutes.
whyHtml:
Most of the useful work in the book starts with the tool reading something you already have: a report, a deck, a spreadsheet, a photo of a whiteboard. And most of it ends with the tool handing you something you can open somewhere else. If you've only ever typed into the box and read what came back, you've used about a third of what's there.

The habit is small: attach the thing instead of describing it. People describe a spreadsheet in three paragraphs when they could attach it in one click, and the description is always worse than the file. The tool reads PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, plain text, and images, and it reads them well enough to quote a page number back to you.

The other half is getting things out. A draft that lives only in the chat is a draft you'll lose. A draft downloaded as a file is yours.
exampleHtml:
The investor deck morning in Chapter 10 started with four files attached: our full company overview, a shorter deck from the week before, an advisor deck, and a PDF of an older investor deck. The tool read all four and built from them. It also read the speaker notes inside one of them, which is how it caught a slide that should never have gone outside the company. I'd have missed that. The notes were in the file; I'd attached the file; it read the whole file.

Going out, the deck came back as both a PowerPoint and a PDF, and I checked the rendered PDF before anything went anywhere, because the rendered file is what the reader sees and the chat's description of it is not.

The thing I didn't know in my first year: it reads images. A photo of a whiteboard after a meeting, attached, comes back as a typed list of what was on the board. I use that most weeks now.

yourTurn.question: Attach a document you already have
yourTurn.html: Attach a document you already have. A PDF or a Word file, anything real. Ask: "Summarize this in five lines and tell me the page number of the most important sentence." Did it get the page right? (Yes or no, and the page.)
yourTurn.expected: Yes or no, and the page

yourTurn.question: Paste a passage
yourTurn.html: Paste a passage. Copy three paragraphs from anything and paste them into the chat with: "What's the weakest claim in this, and why?" Note whether the answer surprised you. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Attach a spreadsheet or a photo
yourTurn.html: Attach a spreadsheet or a photo. A spreadsheet: ask for the three largest numbers in one column. A photo of handwriting or a whiteboard: ask for it typed out. Write what it got wrong, if anything. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Get something out
yourTurn.html: Get something out. Ask for a one-page summary of the document from question 1 as a file. Download it. Open it outside the chat. Write where it landed on your computer. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Your rule for files
yourTurn.html: Your rule for files. Finish this sentence: "When I have the document, I will ______ instead of describing it." (One line.)

howToHtml: How to: attaching and downloading, as of October 20, 2026. In the chat box there's a "+" (or a paperclip) for attaching files; you can also drag a file onto the chat or paste text directly. The tool reads PDFs, Word documents, spreadsheets, plain text, code, and images, within size limits that change; if a file is refused, split it or paste the part you need. Anything it builds opens in a panel beside the chat; documents and decks there have an Export control, and legacy outputs have a download control at the top of the panel; both are also saved to the Artifacts tab in the sidebar. Creating files requires "Code execution and file creation" to be on under Settings > Capabilities. All plans can attach files and create them.
compoundsHtml: Every worksheet in Part B starts by attaching something real: last week's report, your brand guide, a draft. Once attaching is a reflex, the tool is working on your actual material instead of your description of it, and every skill you build in Part B is tested on real files from day one.

title: What an .md file is
promiseText: Read and write one plain-text file with a few symbols for headings and lists, and understand why every skill, rule, and draft in this workbook lives in that format. Fifteen minutes.
promiseHtml: Read and write one plain-text file with a few symbols for headings and lists, and understand why every skill, rule, and draft in this workbook lives in that format. Fifteen minutes.
whyHtml:
Every chapter of the two books was drafted as an .md file. Every skill I've built is one. The voice rules, the brand page, the corrections log, the agent job descriptions: .md files, all of them. If there's one piece of technical knowledge the book asks of you, it's this one, and it's about ten lines of symbols.

An .md file (the letters stand for Markdown) is plain text. You can open it in any program that opens text, on any computer, forever. It has no hidden formatting, no fonts, nothing that depends on one company's software staying in business. The few symbols it uses tell a reader, human or machine, where the headings are and what's a list. That's it.

The reason it matters for this work: the tool reads .md perfectly, writes it by default, and treats the structure as meaning. A heading called "Rules" is a section the tool knows to obey. A list under "Never" is a list it knows not to do. Chapter 11 said to keep what you've learned somewhere that survives the platform. This is the somewhere.
exampleHtml:
Here is the top of one of my skill files, exactly as it's written. The symbols are the whole lesson.

# Skill: Growth Brief post

This skill serves Mark. Use it when I say "write the brief."

yourTurn.question: Open a plain-text editor
yourTurn.html: Open a plain-text editor. On a Mac, TextEdit (set to plain text), or any code editor. On Windows, Notepad. Write the name of the one you'll use. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Write your first .md file
yourTurn.html:
Write your first .md file. Type this, with your own words in place of mine, and save it as about-me.md:

# About me

## Who I am
One or two sentences.

## What I'm working on
- First thing
- Second thing

## How I like work done
- One rule

yourTurn.question: Attach it to a conversation
yourTurn.html: Attach it to a conversation (Worksheet 0.2) and ask: "Read this and tell me the three section headings." If it names them, you've written a file the tool can navigate. (Yes or no.)

yourTurn.question: Make your folder
yourTurn.html: Make your folder. One folder for everything from this workbook, with subfolders: skills, notes, logs. Write the path. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: The ten lines
yourTurn.html:
The ten lines. Copy this table somewhere you'll see it until you don't need it:

Symbol Means
# Title The title, once at the top
## Heading A section
### Smaller heading A subsection
- item A list item
1. item A numbered list item
blank line New paragraph
**bold** Bold
`code` Code or a filename
> quote A quoted block
[text](link) A link

howToHtml: How to: .md files, as of October 20, 2026. Any text editor writes them; save with the .md extension. The tool accepts them as attachments on every plan and writes them when you ask for "a markdown file." Skills on Claude.ai are a folder containing a file named SKILL.md, zipped and uploaded under Customize > Skills (Worksheet 0.5 has the steps). You don't need a special program to read one; the symbols are readable as-is.
compoundsHtml: Every file from here on is one of these, and every one of them outlives the conversation it was made in. The about-me.md you just wrote is the first draft of Worksheet A1, and the folder you made is where your skills (Part B) and your agent job descriptions (Part C) will live.

title: Organizing conversations, projects, and memory
promiseText: Start a conversation on purpose, make one project, and see what memory carries between rooms, so you know where everything you tell the tool ends up. Thirty minutes.
promiseHtml: Start a conversation on purpose, make one project, and see what memory carries between rooms, so you know where everything you tell the tool ends up. Thirty minutes.
whyHtml:
Chapters 11 and 12 made the argument: a conversation is a room, and nothing follows you out unless you've set up something to carry it. Three things can. Memory carries what's true about you. A project carries what's true about one body of work. A skill carries how to do one kind of task. This page sets up the first two. Part B sets up the third.

The three sorting questions from Chapter 12 are the whole method, so here they are again. Is this true about me regardless of what I'm working on? Memory. Is this about one body of work, and only that? The project. Is this about how to do one kind of task, wherever it comes up? A skill. If you ask those three questions every time you're about to tell the tool something you'll want it to keep, you'll never explain yourself from scratch again.

The trap is treating them as the same thing. Project facts in memory means every conversation about dinner knows about your Q3 pipeline. Personal preferences in a project means you repeat them in the next project. Sort first.
exampleHtml:
My memory holds who I am and how I like work done: my career with dates, which email to use for which business, the "hundreds of partnerships" wording, the em-dash ban, the rule that anything in my voice gets the humanize pass. Every one of those started as a correction in a conversation and crossed over when I'd said it more than once in more than one room.

I keep two kinds of things out. Anything a stranger shouldn't see on a screen, and anything about other people that's theirs. Memory is for durable, shareable facts about how I work. It isn't a diary.

My projects are rooms with furniture. The book project's instructions say what the book is for and who it's for; its files are the outline, my notes on my own history, the glossary, and the skills that draft the chapters. Open a conversation inside it and the tool already knows all of that. The company has a different project with different furniture. When something from one belongs in the other, I carry it across on purpose, as a file. The web service I'm building got its own project the day it stopped being a book idea, and the handoff was three files and four minutes.

yourTurn.question: Check memory
yourTurn.html: Check memory. Open Settings > Memory. Is "Generate memory from chats" on? Read what it holds under Topics. Write down one thing it has right and one thing it has wrong or missing. (Two lines.)

yourTurn.question: Give it one durable fact
yourTurn.html: Give it one durable fact. In a new conversation, type: "Remember this about me:" followed by one sentence that's true regardless of what you're working on (what you do, or one rule for how you like work done). Then open a second new conversation and ask it what it knows about you. Did the fact carry? (Yes or no.)

yourTurn.question: Sort five things
yourTurn.html: Sort five things. Write five things you've told the tool more than once. Beside each, write M (memory), P (project), or S (skill).

yourTurn.question: Make one project
yourTurn.html: Make one project. Pick one body of work you're in the middle of. Create a project for it. Write two or three sentences of instructions (what it is, who it's for, how you want the tool to behave in it). Add the two files you keep re-attaching. Write the project's name. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Test the room
yourTurn.html: Test the room. Open a new conversation inside the project and ask for something you'd normally have to explain first. Write what you didn't have to say. (Two lines.)

yourTurn.question: Your rule for one-off conversations
yourTurn.html: Your rule for one-off conversations. From Worksheet 0.1: when something in a one-off conversation matters, where does it go, and by when? (One sentence.)

howToHtml: How to: memory and projects, as of October 20, 2026, from the Claude help center. Memory: Settings > Memory, toggle "Generate memory from chats." Everything it remembers is listed under Topics; select one to read, edit, or delete it, or tell the tool in a chat to remember, change, or forget something and it applies from the next conversation. Sensitive topics (health, politics) are excluded unless you turn on "Include sensitive topics in memory." To keep one chat out of memory, click "+" in a new chat and turn off Memory before the first message, or use the ghost icon for an incognito chat. Turning memory off offers "Pause memory" (keeps what's saved, stops using it) or "Reset memory" (deletes everything, including project memories, permanently). Memory is on by default for Free, Pro, and Max; on Team and Enterprise an owner must enable it first. Each project has its own memory plus your account memory; "Use account memory" on the project page turns the account part off for that project. Projects: Projects in the left sidebar, "+ New Project," name and describe it, then "Set project instructions" and the "+" under project knowledge to add files; any chat started inside the project uses both. Free accounts get five projects; paid plans, unlimited. Past-chat search ("Search and reference chats" under Settings > Memory) is on paid plans only.
compoundsHtml: The fact you gave memory in question 2 is the first line of Worksheet A1, and the project you made in question 4 is where every Part B skill gets tested. From here on, each conversation starts closer to where the last one ended, and the explaining you did this week is explaining you won't do next week.

title: Artifacts and outputs
promiseText: Edit, save, and share one thing the tool built for you, and know where a skill lives once you've written one, with the no-setup fallback that works everywhere. Twenty minutes.
promiseHtml: Edit, save, and share one thing the tool built for you, and know where a skill lives once you've written one, with the no-setup fallback that works everywhere. Twenty minutes.
whyHtml:
When the tool makes something substantial (a document, a page, a deck, a small tool), it doesn't put it in the chat. It opens it in a panel beside the chat, saves it, and lets you come back to it, change it, and share it. The help pages call these artifacts. The book mostly calls them "the thing it built," because that's what they are.

Two habits here. First: anything you'll keep, you edit in the panel and export, because the rendered file is what a reader sees and the chat's description of it is not (Chapter 10 learned this the hard way). Second: a skill you've written (Part B) has to live somewhere the tool will load it. There's a proper place, and there's a fallback that works on every plan with no setup, and you should know both, because the proper place has moved more than once and will again.
exampleHtml:
The investor deck came back as an artifact: fourteen slides in a panel beside the chat, rebuilt twenty-three times, each version rendered so I could read it as the investor would. I exported the PDF to send and kept the PowerPoint as the source. Both are in the Artifacts tab if I need them again, and I've gone back to that tab for a deck more than once.

My skills live in two places. The saved version is uploaded under Customize > Skills, where the tool loads it whenever I name the task. The source is the .md file in my skills folder on my own computer, and that's the one I edit, because the file is mine and the upload is a copy. When a skill changes, I upload the new version and the old one is gone. Before I had saved skills, I pasted the instructions at the top of every conversation, which is slower and works exactly as well. If the upload button moves tomorrow, pasting still works.

yourTurn.question: Build one thing
yourTurn.html: Build one thing. Ask for a one-page document on anything you know well: "Write a one-page explainer on [topic] as a document." Watch where it opens. (Write the panel's position: beside the chat, or somewhere else.)
yourTurn.expected: Write the panel's position: beside the chat, or somewhere else

yourTurn.question: Edit it two ways
yourTurn.html: Edit it two ways. First, ask the chat for one change. Then make one change directly in the panel. Which felt more natural? (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Export it
yourTurn.html: Export it. Use the Export control to download it as a Word file or PDF. Open the download. Write the filename. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Find it again tomorrow
yourTurn.html: Find it again tomorrow. Open the Artifacts tab in the sidebar and confirm it's there. (Yes or no.)

yourTurn.question: Place your first skill, two ways
yourTurn.html:
Place your first skill, two ways. Take the about-me.md from Worksheet 0.3 (or any instructions you'd give the tool every time).

  • Fallback, works everywhere: start a new conversation, paste the whole file at the top, then ask for the task. Write whether it followed the rules. (One line.)
  • Saved skill: follow the sidebar below to upload it. Then start a fresh conversation, don't paste anything, and ask for the task. Did it load? (Yes or no.)

yourTurn.question: Your rule
yourTurn.html: Your rule. Finish: "Anything I'll keep, I ______ before I send it." (The answer is in Chapter 10.)

howToHtml: How to: artifacts and skills, as of October 20, 2026, from the Claude help center. Artifacts open beside the chat and are saved to the Artifacts tab in the sidebar; they start private. Document, deck, and design artifacts have an Export control (documents to Word, PDF, Markdown, or Google Docs; decks to PowerPoint or PDF; designs to zip, PDF, PowerPoint, or HTML); older-style artifacts have view, copy, and download controls at the top of the panel. In a document, highlight text and choose "Edit with Claude" to change a passage. Creating artifacts requires "Code execution and file creation" on under Settings > Capabilities; it's available on every plan, with the template kinds (Docs, Slides, Design) on paid plans. Skills: put your SKILL.md in a folder named for the skill, zip the folder, go to Customize > Skills, click "+", then "+ Create skill," then "Upload a skill." Each skill has an on/off toggle there. Skills are available on every plan and need code execution turned on. If an upload fails, the usual reasons are a folder name that doesn't match the skill name, a missing SKILL.md, or an odd character in the name. The fallback, pasting the file at the top of a conversation, needs nothing.
compoundsHtml: You now have the two moves every later worksheet assumes: get the rendered thing out before you ship it, and put a skill where the tool loads it without being asked. Part B's first worksheet ends with you uploading a real skill using exactly step 5, and Chapter 11's re-test routine assumes you know where your skills live.

title: Five settings worth knowing
promiseText: A dated table of the five settings that change what the tool does for you, checked once so you stop wondering why it behaved differently today. Ten minutes.
promiseHtml: A dated table of the five settings that change what the tool does for you, checked once so you stop wondering why it behaved differently today. Ten minutes.
whyHtml:
Most of what people blame on the tool is a setting. It didn't search the web because search was off for that chat. It didn't remember because memory was paused. It gave a shallower answer because a faster model was selected. It couldn't make a file because file creation wasn't turned on. None of those is the tool being bad at the job. All of them are a toggle.

Five settings account for nearly every "it worked yesterday" I've heard, so this page is a table and a check. Go through it once. Then, when something behaves oddly, come back here before you blame yourself or the machine.

Chapter 11 warned that these move. The table has a date on it. If the date is old, the names may have changed; the setting itself almost certainly still exists, so ask the tool where it is now.
exampleHtml:
The setting that cost me the most was web search, early on. I'd ask for a figure, get a confident number, and only later work out that search had been off and the number came from the model's memory of the world, with the world itself never consulted. Now I check the slider when a fact matters, and Chapter 6's pass assumes search is on.

The one I changed most recently was model choice. For a year I ran the strongest model for everything. I still do for judgment work: drafting, arguing, anything with a reader who matters. For routine summaries I've moved down a tier, because the wait and the usage limit started to cost me more than the difference in quality. The right setting changes with the job in front of you.

yourTurn.html: Go through the table. For each row, find the setting, note where it is today, and set it the way you want it. Write a word in the last column.

cells: Whether it looks things up live, with citations, or answers from what it learned in training. On when facts matter.
The slider icon in the chat box, "Web search" toggle; per chat
Whether it keeps and uses what it knows about you between conversations
Settings > Memory, "Generate memory from chats"; pause or reset from the same toggle
Whether it can look back through your earlier conversations when you ask
Settings > Memory, "Search and reference chats" (paid plans)
Which model answers: the strongest for judgment, a faster one for routine work
The model picker in the chat box; which models you see depends on plan
Whether it can build documents, decks, pages, and run code
Settings > Capabilities, "Code execution and file creation"

yourTurn.html: Then two questions:

yourTurn.question: Which of the five was set differently from how you expected?
yourTurn.html: Which of the five was set differently from how you expected? (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Your check
yourTurn.html: Your check. When an answer surprises you, which row will you look at first? (One line. Mine is web search.)
yourTurn.expected: One line. Mine is web search

howToHtml: How to: settings, as of October 20, 2026, from the Claude help center and claude.com. Web search is per chat and counts against usage on free accounts. Memory is on by default on Free, Pro, and Max and must be enabled by an owner on Team and Enterprise. Past-chat search is on paid plans. Models by plan, per claude.com/pricing: Free has Sonnet and Haiku; Pro adds Opus and the Fable model through usage credits; Max and Team premium seats include Fable at a share of weekly limits. Where preferences live: Settings > Memory for what it remembers about you; a project's instructions for how it behaves in that project; your skills for how it does a task. All three are the places Worksheet 0.4 sorted things into.
compoundsHtml: You've turned five mysteries into five known switches. From now on, a strange answer costs you thirty seconds of checking instead of an afternoon of doubt, and when Chapter 11's next change arrives, you'll know which switch to look for instead of relearning the tool.

title: Models and platform changes
promiseText: A dated table of the current models and which to use for what, a one-page change log you'll keep, and the hour-long re-test routine for the day a new model lands. Thirty minutes to set up; an hour each time it's needed.
promiseHtml: A dated table of the current models and which to use for what, a one-page change log you'll keep, and the hour-long re-test routine for the day a new model lands. Thirty minutes to set up; an hour each time it's needed.
whyHtml:
Chapter 11 said the platform moves. This is the page that keeps you standing when it does.

Three things on it. A table of today's models, dated, so you know what you're choosing between and which to pick for which work. A change log, which is a half-page file you add a line to whenever the tool changes under you. And the re-test routine: the hour you spend after a release running your most-used skills against a real task and comparing to the last thing you approved, so drift gets caught by you, on purpose, instead of by a reader, by accident.

None of this is technical. The hardest part is remembering to do it, which is why the log has a date column and the first line in it is today.
exampleHtml:
My log started after the first time a release broke a skill without telling me. My column skill, tuned over months, started producing longer paragraphs and a phrase I'd never had to ban before. It took me a day to work out that the model had changed and my file hadn't. The log is three lines per release now: date, model, what I changed. I've been glad of it every time.

The re-test is an hour. Three skills (column, voice pass, deck), one real task each, compare to the last version I approved. If something drifted, fix the file, not the draft. Read the release notes for anything about writing style or tools. Log it. Since the Logitech years, when every operating-system release meant re-testing every product, I haven't found a better routine than test before, test after, write down what moved.

Which model for what, as I do it today: the strongest for anything with a reader who matters or a judgment call in it; a faster tier for summaries, sorting, and first passes I'll check anyway. A good brief outranks the tier. The weak model with four hundred words of context beats the strong one with four.

yourTurn.question: Copy the model table
yourTurn.html:
Copy the model table into your notes folder as models.md, with today's date at the top. Cross out rows as they retire; add rows as they arrive.

Model (as of October 20, 2026) What Anthropic calls it What I use it for
Fable 5.1 "Next generation intelligence for long-running agents" Judgment work, long documents, hard arguments
Opus 5.5 "Daily driver for agentic coding and enterprise work" Drafting and building; the default on paid plans
Sonnet 5.5 "High-performance model for coding and agents" Routine drafts, summaries, sorting
Haiku 5.5 "Fastest, most cost-efficient model" Quick questions, bulk work I'll check

Write your own third column. (Four lines.)

yourTurn.question: Start your change log
yourTurn.html:
Start your change log. Create logs/platform-changes.md in your folder with this header and one line for today:

# Platform changes
| Date | What changed | What I did about it |
|---|---|---|
| 2026-10-20 | Started this log; models as of today in models.md | Nothing yet |

yourTurn.question: Pick your three
yourTurn.html: Pick your three. Which three skills or routines would you re-test after a release? If you don't have skills yet, which three tasks do you ask for most? (Three lines.)

yourTurn.question: Write the routine
yourTurn.html: Write the routine as you'll run it, in your words, under an hour:

fields.label: Run each of the three on a real task
Compare to the last result I approved
If something drifted, fix the file, not the draft

yourTurn.question: Set a trigger
yourTurn.html: Set a trigger. How will you find out a new model has landed? (The model picker changes; the tool often announces it; a colleague mentions it.) Write the one you'll rely on. (One line.)

howToHtml: How to: models and releases, as of October 20, 2026, from claude.com/pricing. Four current models are offered: Fable 5.1, Opus 5.5, Sonnet 5.5, and Haiku 5.5; older versions remain listed as legacy for a time. Free accounts use Sonnet and Haiku; Pro adds Opus and Fable through usage credits; Max and Team premium seats include Fable at a share of weekly limits. A new release usually appears in the model picker in the chat box and in Anthropic's announcements; the previous model stays available for a while and then retires. A separate Mythos tier exists and is not generally available. Treat every name in this sidebar as provisional; the table in question 1 is yours to keep current.
compoundsHtml: Every release after this one costs you an hour instead of a lost week, and the log turns each change into a line you can read back when a draft feels off. Your skills (Part B) survive because you re-test them; your voice (Part A) stays yours because drift gets caught the week it happens, not the month after.

title: The paragraph about you
promiseText: The 150 words you give the AI once, so every conversation starts knowing who you are, what you know, and what you're working on. Thirty minutes.
promiseHtml: The 150 words you give the AI once, so every conversation starts knowing who you are, what you know, and what you're working on. Thirty minutes.
whyHtml:
Chapter 1 said the quality of the answer is set by what you give before you ask. The first thing to give is you. Not a résumé. The two or three things about your experience that should change how the tool reasons with you, what you're trying to do, and what you'd want a smart new colleague to know on day one.

I spent a year getting generic answers because I never said who I was. The morning that changed, in Chapter 1, I typed four hundred words before asking anything, and the first hundred were about me: a coffee company at 23, hundreds of store openings, what retail labor costs. The tool stopped explaining retail to me and started reasoning with me. That paragraph is the one you'll write here, and Chapter 12 showed where it lives so you never type it again.

Keep it to what you'd be comfortable with a colleague reading on a screen. This is the durable, shareable version of you. It isn't a diary, and it isn't the place for anything you'd keep out of a work email.
exampleHtml:
Here's mine, as it stands today. It's changed a dozen times and it'll change again.

I'm Mark Anderson. I run revenue at a security company that builds trust infrastructure for AI agents, and I run a small consultancy on the side. I've spent thirty years building and growing companies: a coffee company I started at 23, a big coffee chain's expansion from under 300 stores to over 1,000, an internet bank in 1997, then hardware and software companies where I built hundreds of partnerships, including one with Google that put our touch technology into a product they shipped. I know go-to-market, partnerships, and what it costs to open a location or sign an enterprise deal. I'm working on two books about using AI and on a web service that grows out of them. I think in facts and reasonable conclusions, I'd rather you be direct and let me decide than lay out options and wait, and I'll tell you when you're wrong. [MARK: tighten this to the version you'd actually hand it.]

What's in it: who I am, in one line; the experience that should change how it reasons (the operator's view of retail, partnerships, enterprise sales); what I'm working on now; how to work with me. What's not in it: anything about money, health, family, or other people.

yourTurn.html: Write each piece, then assemble the paragraph.

yourTurn.question: Who you are, in one line
yourTurn.html: Who you are, in one line. Role and the kind of work, no company history yet.

yourTurn.question: Two or three things you know from experience
yourTurn.html: Two or three things you know from experience that should change how it reasons with you. Not titles. The thing you'd say to stop someone explaining your own field to you.

yourTurn.question: What you're working on now
yourTurn.html: What you're working on now. One or two things, in a sentence each.

yourTurn.question: How to work with you
yourTurn.html: How to work with you. One or two lines: direct or thorough, options or a recommendation, push back or defer.

yourTurn.question: Assemble it
yourTurn.html: Assemble it. Put 1 through 4 into one paragraph, 100 to 150 words, in your own voice. Read it aloud. Cut anything you wouldn't say to a new colleague on day one.

yourTurn.question: Give it to the tool
yourTurn.html: Give it to the tool. In a new conversation: "Remember this about me:" and paste the paragraph. Then open another new conversation and ask what it knows about you. Fix anything it got wrong. Then save the paragraph as about-me.md in your notes folder, because the file is yours and the memory is a copy.

howToHtml: How to: where the paragraph lives, as of October 20, 2026. Memory (Settings > Memory, "Generate memory from chats") carries it between conversations on Free, Pro, and Max; on Team and Enterprise an owner enables memory first. You can also paste it at the top of any conversation, which works on every plan with no setup. If you keep the paragraph in a project's instructions instead, it applies only inside that project; memory is the right home for the parts that are true everywhere. Worksheet 0.4 has the details.
compoundsHtml: This paragraph is the first hundred words of every brief you'll ever write, and you just wrote it for the last time. Worksheet A2 builds the rest of the brief on top of it, and A3 refines the "how to work with me" line into ten.

title: Your brief, every time
promiseText: A five-part frame you fill in before any real task, with one real brief completed and tested. Forty minutes.
promiseHtml: A five-part frame you fill in before any real task, with one real brief completed and tested. Forty minutes.
whyHtml:
Four hundred words beats four. Chapter 1 said it and every chapter after it depended on it. The difference between the generic retail report I got in my first year and the business plan I got a year later wasn't the tool. It was the brief: who I was, who the work was for, what I was actually trying to do, what I'd already tried, and what good looked like. Then the ask, in one sentence.

The frame is the same every time, which is why it belongs on a page you can copy. After a few weeks you won't need the page; the shape will be in your hands. Until then, fill it in.

One thing to expect. The first answer to a good brief is often still the easy answer, the one the tool reaches for by habit. Chapter 1's second lesson was to stay in the conversation and correct it. The brief gets you a better first draft; the correction gets you the real one.
exampleHtml:
The brief that opened Chapter 1, condensed to its parts. The real one was four hundred words.

Who I am and what I know. Ran a coffee company at 23. Helped open hundreds of Starbucks stores. I know what retail labor costs, what a lease does to you, what a slow Tuesday looks like.

Who the work is for. Me, first, to decide whether this concept can work. Then a business partner who'll want the numbers.

What I'm trying to do. Not "research this market." Find out whether a model exists for this concept that doesn't break on retail's margins, and if so, what it looks like.

What I've tried and what I don't want. I've asked this before and got a generic report on why retail is hard. I know why retail is hard. Don't give me that.

What good looks like. A model that works on paper, with the math shown, and a note on every assumption I'd have to prove.

The ask. Build me the unit economics for this concept, one location at a time, and show me where it breaks.

Then, when it came back generic anyway: the capital-and-labor problem isn't a reason to stop, it's the thing to design around; assume one central kitchen and partner locations; rebuild the model on that. That correction was the whole morning.

yourTurn.html: Pick one real task you need done this week. Fill in the frame for it. Then run it.

yourTurn.question: Who I am and what I know
yourTurn.html: Who I am and what I know (two or three lines; A1's paragraph does most of this, so add only what matters for this task):
yourTurn.expected: two or three lines; A1's paragraph does most of this, so add only what matters for this task

yourTurn.question: Who the work is for
yourTurn.html: Who the work is for (the reader, the customer, the person in the room; one or two lines):
yourTurn.expected: the reader, the customer, the person in the room; one or two lines

yourTurn.question: What I'm actually trying to do
yourTurn.html: What I'm actually trying to do (the goal, not the task; one or two lines):
yourTurn.expected: the goal, not the task; one or two lines

yourTurn.question: What I've tried, and what I don't want
yourTurn.html: What I've tried, and what I don't want (two or three lines; this is the part people skip):
yourTurn.expected: two or three lines; this is the part people skip

yourTurn.question: What good looks like
yourTurn.html: What good looks like (length, tone, format, the one thing it must get right; two lines):
yourTurn.expected: length, tone, format, the one thing it must get right; two lines

yourTurn.question: The ask
yourTurn.html: The ask (one sentence):

yourTurn.question: Run it
yourTurn.html: Run it. Paste 1 through 6 into a new conversation and send. Read the answer. Was it the easy version? Write the one correction you gave it. (One or two lines.)

yourTurn.question: Keep the frame
yourTurn.html: Keep the frame. Save this filled-in brief as briefs/first-brief.md. Save the blank frame as briefs/frame.md. Next time, copy the frame.

howToHtml: How to: nothing to set up. The brief is text you paste. If you've done A1 and Worksheet 0.4, memory already carries part 1, and you can start at part 2. Working inside a project (0.4) carries parts 1 and 2 for everything in that body of work; the task-specific parts (3 through 6) still go in the conversation every time, because they're true only today.
compoundsHtml: Every brief you write makes the next one faster, because parts 1 and 2 stop changing and parts 4 and 5 turn into rules. When the same "what I don't want" shows up three briefs in a row, it goes into the corrections log (A4), and when it shows up in every brief for one kind of task, it goes into a skill (Part B).

title: How you want it to talk to you
promiseText: Ten preference lines (length, tone, format, what to skip, what to never say) ready to paste or save, so the tool's default manner becomes yours. Twenty minutes.
promiseHtml: Ten preference lines (length, tone, format, what to skip, what to never say) ready to paste or save, so the tool's default manner becomes yours. Twenty minutes.
whyHtml:
Chapter 2 said to talk to it like a colleague, and the colleague should learn how you like to be talked to. Most people never say. They get the tool's default manner (eager, thorough, balanced, a little too pleased with itself) and either put up with it or quit. Ten lines fix it.

The lines are about manner, not content. Length: short or complete. Format: prose or lists. Stance: a recommendation or the options. Pushback: argue with me or defer. And the phrases it never uses with you, because you've heard them and they cost it your trust.

Chapter 12 explained why these belong in memory and not in a project: they're true about you regardless of the work. Write them once, give them once, and every room you walk into already knows.
exampleHtml:
Mine, as they stand. Ten lines, and the first three do most of the work.

  1. Be direct and let me decide. One recommendation, then the reasoning. Options only if I ask.
  2. Lead with the deliverable or the answer. No restating my question, no preamble.
  3. Push back when I'm wrong, with the fact that shows it. Don't soften it.
  4. Default to prose. Lists only when I'll scan or compare.
  5. Short when the point is short. Don't pad to look thorough.
  6. Plain words. "Move money," not "execute financial transactions."
  7. Never write "I want to be honest with you" or any sentence that announces sincerity. Say the thing.
  8. No em dashes, anywhere. Commas, periods, colons, parentheses.
  9. Never invent a memory, a quote, a meeting, or a number. Leave a bracket and ask.
  10. When you don't know, say so in one line and tell me what you'd check.

Every one of those started as a correction in a conversation. Number 7 was the first, and the story's in Chapter 2.

yourTurn.html: Write your ten. Use mine as a shape, not a script; half of yours should be different from mine.

yourTurn.question: Stance
yourTurn.html: Stance. A recommendation, or the options? Decide for me, or lay it out?

yourTurn.question: Opening
yourTurn.html: Opening. What should the first line of every answer be?

yourTurn.question: Pushback
yourTurn.html: Pushback. Argue with me, or defer? How hard?

yourTurn.question: Format
yourTurn.html: Format. Prose or lists? When is each right?

yourTurn.question: Length
yourTurn.html: Length. Short by default, or complete by default?

yourTurn.question: Words
yourTurn.html: Words. One rule about vocabulary (plain, technical, no jargon, your field's terms).

yourTurn.question: Never say
yourTurn.html: Never say. One phrase or kind of phrase it must never use with you.

yourTurn.question: Punctuation or style
yourTurn.html: Punctuation or style. One rule, if you have one (mine is em dashes).

yourTurn.question: When it doesn't know
yourTurn.html: When it doesn't know. What should it do?

yourTurn.question: One more
yourTurn.html: One more. The thing that's bothered you most so far.

Then: paste all ten into a new conversation after "Remember how I want you to talk to me:" and, in a second new conversation, ask for something you'd normally get a padded answer to. Did the manner change? Save the ten as preferences.md in your notes folder.

howToHtml: How to: as of October 20, 2026, these lines live best in memory (Settings > Memory; Worksheet 0.4), where they apply in every conversation on Free, Pro, and Max. On every plan they also work pasted at the top of a conversation. Put them in a project's instructions only if you want a different manner for one body of work.
compoundsHtml: Ten lines, given once, change every answer you'll get from now on. And they're the seed of your voice skill in Part B: when the tool writes as you, these are the first rules it follows, and the corrections log in A4 is where the next ten come from.

title: Your corrections log
promiseText: A running list of the corrections that must stick, with the first five filled in and a rule for when a correction graduates into memory or a skill. Twenty minutes to start; two minutes a week after.
promiseHtml: A running list of the corrections that must stick, with the first five filled in and a rule for when a correction graduates into memory or a skill. Twenty minutes to start; two minutes a week after.
whyHtml:
Chapter 2's whole argument fits in one line: every correction you keep is one you never make again. The keeping is the part people skip. They correct the tool in the moment, it holds for the conversation, and the next conversation makes the same mistake (Chapter 11 explained why: a conversation is a room). The log is where the correction goes so it survives the room.

It's a file. One line per correction: what it did, what it should do instead, the date. Nothing else. After a month you'll have twenty lines and you'll notice three things about them: the same correction appears more than once, some of them are about you regardless of the task, and some are about one kind of work. That's the sorting from Chapter 12, and the log is where it happens.

I didn't set out to build a list. I set out to fix one sentence in one draft. The list is longer now, and every item on it started as a second message.
exampleHtml:
The first entries in mine, from memory, with the dates approximate.

Date What it did What it should do Where it went
Early 2026 Wrote "I want to be honest with you" in a column draft Never. Say the thing. Memory, then the voice skill
Spring 2026 Implied I'd worked at Google I built a partnership with Google, from RAPT. I never worked there. Memory, and every book skill
Sept 2026 Wrote "100+ partnerships" "Hundreds of partnerships." Memory
Sept 2026 Em dashes in everything None. Commas, periods, colons, parentheses. Memory, voice skill, the linter
Oct 2026 "Thirty years using computers" "Close to fifty years." The book skills
Oct 2026 Named an investor in a chapter No names of investors, prospects, customers, or colleagues. Roles only. The book skills

The last column is the point. A correction that's true about me everywhere went to memory. A correction about one kind of work went to that skill. The ones that cost me most (the em dashes, that first banned line) got a line in the linter, so a machine catches them before I do.

yourTurn.question: Start the file
yourTurn.html:
Start the file. Create logs/corrections.md with this header:

# Corrections
| Date | What it did | What it should do | Where it went |
|---|---|---|---|

yourTurn.question: Fill in the first five
yourTurn.html: Fill in the first five. Think back over your conversations so far. What have you corrected more than once? Write five rows. Leave the last column blank for now.

yourTurn.question: Sort them
yourTurn.html: Sort them. For each row, ask Chapter 12's questions: true about me everywhere (memory), about one kind of task (a skill, Part B), or true only in one project (that project's instructions)? Fill in the last column with where it should go, even if you haven't put it there yet.

yourTurn.question: Move the first one
yourTurn.html: Move the first one. Take the correction that's bitten you most. If it's a memory item, give it to the tool now ("Remember: never..."). If it's a skill item, keep it; B1 will have a Rules section waiting for it.

yourTurn.question: Set the habit
yourTurn.html: Set the habit. Finish this sentence and put it where you'll see it: "When I correct the tool and I've corrected it before, I ______ within ______." (Mine: add a row the same day.)
yourTurn.expected: Mine: add a row the same day

howToHtml: How to: nothing to install; the log is an .md file in your folder (Worksheet 0.3). Memory items go in through a conversation ("Remember this:") or Settings > Memory; skill items go into the Rules section of the skill's SKILL.md; project items go into the project's instructions. Worksheet 0.4 has the locations as of October 20, 2026.
compoundsHtml: The log is the raw material for everything in Part B. Every rule in your first skill comes from a row here, and every row you add is a correction you'll make once instead of forever. After three months, read the log top to bottom: it's a record of the tool learning you, written by you.

title: Your trust rules
promiseText: Your own rules for what you check and how, in five lines, with one real piece of work checked against them. Thirty minutes.
promiseHtml: Your own rules for what you check and how, in five lines, with one real piece of work checked against them. Thirty minutes.
whyHtml:
Chapter 3 said the tool sounds the same when it's right and when it's wrong. Chapter 6 said the biggest mistake people are making with AI right now is passing along output they never checked, and told you about a friend of mine who's deciding whether to keep people over it. Nothing leaves your hands unchecked. This page turns that from a sentence you agree with into five rules you run.

The rules are yours because the stakes are yours. A number in a deck to an investor needs a different check from a number in a note to yourself. A quote attributed to a public figure needs a different check from a summary of a document you attached. Write the rules for the work you actually send, and make them short enough to run every time.

The last rule on your list should be the three-minute test from Chapter 6: can you explain the thing out loud, with no materials, for three minutes? If you can't, you aren't done. It's the check that catches what the other four miss, because it's a check on you, not on the draft.
exampleHtml:
Mine, in the order I run them on anything with a number, a name, a date, or a quote in it.

  1. Every number has a named source and a date, in the text or in a note. "According to industry data" doesn't count.
  2. Open the source. Read the sentence the number comes from. If I can't find it, the number comes out or gets marked as unverified.
  3. Find the one number the argument turns on and check it twice. One wrong number there costs more than ten wrong numbers elsewhere.
  4. Anything I'll say to someone who knows the subject better than I do gets the whole pass, not the quick one. The investor who knows the competitor's real figures exists for every piece of work.
  5. Before it goes out: three minutes, out loud, no notes. If I can't, it isn't finished.

What I write down at the end of every pass: the line listing what I couldn't verify. That line is the habit. It's the one most people never write, and it's what lets me stand in front of a reader and say "this holds, and here's the one thing I'm not sure of."

yourTurn.question: What do you send that has to be right?
yourTurn.html: What do you send that has to be right? List the three kinds of work where a wrong fact would cost you something real. (Three lines.)

yourTurn.question: Write your five rules
yourTurn.html: Write your five rules. Use mine as a shape. At least two of yours should be specific to the work in question 1.

yourTurn.question: Run them on something real
yourTurn.html: Run them on something real. Take a piece the tool made for you this week with at least three facts in it. Apply all five rules. Mark each fact: confirmed, close but wrong, or couldn't find it. Write the count. (One line.)

yourTurn.question: Write the unverified line
yourTurn.html: Write the unverified line. At the bottom of that piece, one line listing what you couldn't confirm. Copy it here.

yourTurn.question: The three-minute test
yourTurn.html: The three-minute test. Stand up and explain the piece out loud, no materials, for three minutes. Did you make it? What did you stumble on? (Two lines.)

yourTurn.question: Save the rules
yourTurn.html: Save the rules as trust-rules.md in your notes folder, and paste them into memory ("Remember my checking rules:") so the tool knows what you'll hold it to.

howToHtml: How to: as of October 20, 2026, checking needs web search on (the slider in the chat box, "Web search") so the tool can open sources and cite them; ask it for "the source and the sentence the number comes from," then open the link yourself. Worksheet 0.6 has the setting. The three-minute test needs nothing but a door you can close.
compoundsHtml: Part B's fact-check skill (B5) is these five rules written so the tool runs them before you do, and your "unverified" line becomes a standard part of everything it hands you. Each time you catch something, add it to the corrections log (A4). The rules get sharper, the catches get rarer, and the person at the center stays the one who decides what's true.
